gloss_terse: Beside; from (gen.), at/with (dat.), along/beyond (acc.) — marking source, proximity, comparison, or deviation
gloss_readable: One of the most versatile Greek prepositions, para governs all three cases and shifts meaning accordingly. With the genitive it marks source or origin ('from beside'), with the dative it indicates proximity or presence ('beside, with'), and with the accusative it denotes motion alongside, comparison ('more than'), or deviation ('contrary to'). Spanish captures the source sense with 'de parte de,' while French consistently renders the proximity cluster as 'aupres de.' Paul exploits the comparative accusative powerfully in Romans 1:25, where creatures are worshipped 'para the Creator' — beyond, instead of, in violation of the natural order.

senses.1: With the genitive, para marks the point of origin or source from which something proceeds — a person sending, a place of departure. Spanish 'de parte de' and German 'bei' both highlight this relational provenance. In Matt 2:7 Herod inquires 'from' the magi; in Matt 21:42 the rejected stone comes 'from' the Lord. The genitive construction accounts for roughly 80 of 192 NT occurrences.
senses.2: Indicates association, possession, or being in someone's company — 'with' in the sense of 'at one's side.' Spanish renders this as 'con' or 'ante,' French as 'aupres de.' In Matt 19:26 Jesus declares what is impossible 'with men' is possible 'with God,' using para twice with the dative to contrast human limitation with divine capacity.
senses.3: Spatial proximity with the dative: 'beside, near, at the edge of.' In Matt 4:18 Jesus walks 'beside' the Sea of Galilee; in Matt 13:4 seed falls 'along' the path. Spanish 'junto a' and German 'bei' preserve this locative flavor. The sense clusters around bodies of water, roads, and gathering places throughout the Synoptic narratives.
senses.4: With the accusative in comparative constructions, para means 'than, beyond, more than.' Luke 13:2 asks whether certain Galileans were sinners 'beyond' all others. Romans 1:25 intensifies this to 'instead of' — worshipping the creature 'para the Creator.' Spanish 'mas alla de' captures the sense of exceeding a standard or crossing a boundary.
senses.5: Denotes being in someone's judgment, estimation, or evaluative presence — 'before, in the sight of.' Romans 2:11 declares no partiality 'with God' (para theo), and 1 Cor 3:19 says worldly wisdom is foolishness 'before God.' German 'bei' and French 'aupres de' both carry this evaluative nuance. The sense overlaps with sense 2 but emphasizes appraisal rather than companionship.
senses.6: Expresses contrariety or deviation from an expected norm — 'contrary to, against.' Romans 1:26 speaks of passions 'para nature,' and Romans 16:17 warns against those acting 'contrary to' received teaching. Spanish 'contra' isolates this adversative force clearly. All five occurrences cluster in Paul's epistles, reflecting his fondness for para with the accusative to mark theological deviation.
senses.7: Indicates distribution or location among a group — 'among, in the midst of.' In Matt 28:15 the story spreads 'among' the Jews; in Rev 2:13 Antipas is martyred 'among' you where Satan dwells. Spanish 'entre' and the English 'among' distinguish this from simple proximity. The sense appears in narrative contexts describing communal reception or reputation.
senses.8: Marks exclusion or exception — 'apart from, besides, except.' In 1 Cor 3:11 no one can lay a foundation 'apart from' the one already laid. 2 Cor 11:24 uses it arithmetically: forty lashes 'minus' one. Spanish 'aparte de' and English 'besides' convey this limiting force. All four occurrences appear in the Pauline corpus.
senses.9: A residual pair in 1 Cor 12:15-16 where para introduces the reason or basis for group membership ('for that reason'), rendered in Spanish as 'por' and English as 'for.' The usage is unusual and may reflect an elliptical comparative or causal extension of the accusative 'alongside' sense applied to the body-of-Christ metaphor.

gloss_terse: Discern, understand, perceive; give or gain insight — spanning sensory perception, intellectual grasp, and instruction
gloss_readable: A root at the heart of biblical wisdom literature, bin covers the full arc from raw perception to refined discernment. In the Qal it means to perceive or understand; the Niphal participle yields the classic adjective 'discerning, prudent' (Gen 41:33); the Hifil serves double duty as both 'to possess understanding' and 'to cause another to understand.' Arabic fahima and Ethiopic bayyana share this same semantic core of distinguishing and making clear. The Hitpael adds a reflective dimension — the deliberate act of pondering, as when Job considers God's ways (Job 23:15).

senses.1: The foundational Qal sense: to perceive, understand, or comprehend a matter through cognitive engagement. Arabic fahima and Swahili kuelewa both capture this basic grasp. In 1 Sam 3:8 the priest Eli 'understood' that the Lord was calling the boy; in Neh 8:8 the people 'understood' the reading of the Torah. This is bin at its most general — the moment insight arrives.
senses.2: The Hifil used statively to describe possessing understanding or exercising intelligence — not causing it in another but having it oneself. Korean 분별하는 자 ('one who discerns') reflects this well. Solomon's request in 1 Kgs 3:11 and the skilled Levitical musicians of 1 Chr 25:7-8 exemplify this sense: people characterized by settled, practiced understanding rather than a single flash of insight.
senses.3: The Hifil in its properly causative role: to make someone understand, to instruct or teach. Arabic fahhama ('cause to comprehend') maps precisely. Ezra 8:16 sends for men who can 'cause understanding'; in Neh 8:7-9 the Levites 'cause the people to understand' the Torah. This pedagogical sense is the engine of Israelite wisdom transmission.
senses.4: The Niphal participle functioning adjectivally: 'discerning, prudent, intelligent.' Pharaoh seeks a man 'discerning and wise' in Gen 41:33; Moses selects leaders who are 'wise, discerning, and experienced' in Deut 1:13. Arabic fahim and Korean 총명한 both capture this attributive quality. The form became nearly a technical term for wisdom-qualified leadership.
senses.5: The Hitpael reflexive-intensive: to consider deliberately, reflect, ponder. Arabic ta'ammala and Swahili -tafakari convey this careful, often prolonged meditation. Job 23:15 shows Job 'considering' and growing terrified; Eccl 7:25 has Qoheleth 'considering' to find wisdom. The stem signals that understanding here is effortful, self-directed, and ongoing.
senses.6: A Qal sub-sense of directing attention or giving regard — not full comprehension but focused observation. In Prov 7:7 the sage 'observed' among the simple youths; in Ps 5:1 the psalmist asks God to 'give attention' to his groaning. Korean 살피다 ('examine closely') captures the investigative quality that distinguishes this from the broader sense 1.
senses.7: Infinitival usage (Qal and Hifil) expressing the abstract concept or purpose of understanding. Solomon asks for a heart 'to understand' justice (1 Kgs 3:9); Ps 94:8 challenges the brutish 'to understand.' Arabic fahm ('comprehension' as a noun/infinitive) parallels this abstraction. The form often appears in purpose clauses or wisdom maxims defining the goal of the wise life.
senses.8: A single occurrence in 2 Chr 11:23 where Rehoboam 'acted wisely' in distributing his sons across Judah's fortified cities. English 'acted wisely' and Spanish 'entendio' suggest a pragmatic, strategic sense — understanding translated into shrewd action. This may represent a Hifil elative use pushed toward practical sagacity rather than theoretical comprehension.
senses.9: A unique occurrence in Deut 32:10 where God 'cared for' or 'watched over' Israel in the wilderness. Multilingual evidence (English 'he cared for him,' Spanish 'lo cuido') points away from cognitive understanding toward protective attention. Placed in the Song of Moses alongside surrounding and guarding, this usage extends bin's perceptual core into the domain of nurturing vigilance.

gloss_terse: Turn about, go around, surround; change direction or cause redirection — covering circuits, sieges, and transformations
gloss_readable: A kinetic root whose basic image is circular or rotational motion. In the Qal, sabab can mean to turn oneself (Gen 42:24, where Joseph turns away to weep), to surround an enemy (Judg 20:5), or to march around a city (Josh 6:3). The Hifil adds causative force — turning someone's heart or diverting an army's route. The Niphal describes borders that 'wind around,' while the Piel intensifies the encirclement, as in Ps 32:10 where steadfast love 'surrounds' the one who trusts. Arabic sabab ('rope, means of connection') hints at the root's underlying image of something that wraps or links.

senses.1: Intransitive turning of a subject in the Qal: changing direction, turning around or aside, withdrawing. Arabic iltafata ('turn one's face') captures this well. Joseph 'turned away' to weep in Gen 42:24; Saul's kingdom 'turned' to David (1 Sam 15:27 symbolically). This sense emphasizes the pivot point — the moment a person or entity reverses or redirects.
senses.2: Qal sense of surrounding or encompassing — encircling a person, city, or object. The cords of death 'surrounded' the psalmist (Ps 18:5); Shechemites 'surrounded' Abimelech's house (Judg 9:43). Arabic ahata ('encompass') and Spanish 'rodearon' both map here. The sense covers hostile besieging, protective enclosure, and neutral geographical encirclement alike.
senses.3: Qal sense of traversing a circuit — going around, patrolling, or marching about an area. Joshua's forces 'went around' Jericho (Josh 6:3); Israel 'went around' Edom (Num 21:4). Arabic tafa ('make a circuit') parallels the processional and military dimensions. The emphasis falls on the path traveled rather than what is enclosed.
senses.4: Hifil causative: to turn something or someone, to divert, redirect, or transform. Elijah prays that God will 'turn back' the people's hearts (1 Kgs 18:37); Absalom's advisor seeks to 'turn' the situation (2 Sam 14:20). Arabic hawwala ('change, transfer') captures the transformative force. This sense governs both physical reorientation and metaphorical change of allegiance.
senses.5: Niphal middle-voice turning: borders 'wind around,' boundaries shift direction of their own accord. In Num 34:4-5 the southern boundary of Canaan 'turns' toward the Wadi of Egypt. Gen 19:4 has the men of Sodom 'surrounding' Lot's house in a Niphal that emphasizes the crowd assembling as if of one mind. Arabic imtadda ('extend, stretch') suits the geographical instances.
senses.6: Piel intensive: to surround closely, to circle ceremonially or repeatedly. In Ps 26:6 the psalmist 'goes around' the altar; in Deut 32:10 God 'encircled' Israel protectively in the wilderness. Spanish 'lo rodeo' and the Arabic intensive dawwara both suggest thoroughness or intensity of the encirclement. Cultic procession and divine guardianship merge in this stem.
senses.7: Hifil in its transferential sense: to bring something around, lead around, relocate, or remove from one place to another. The ark is 'brought around' from city to city in 1 Sam 5:8-10; God 'led Israel around' by the wilderness road in Exod 13:18. Arabic naqala ('transfer') and adara ('circulate') both apply. The physical circuit serves the goal of relocation.
senses.8: A rare Qal extension into metaphorical change of state: transformation or alteration of condition. In Zech 14:10 the land 'will be changed' into a plain; in 1 Sam 22:22 David says he has 'caused' (or 'been the occasion of') something turning disastrously. Arabic tahawwala ('be transformed') fits. Only two occurrences suggest this is a marginal but genuine semantic extension.
senses.9: Hofal passive: to be turned or changed by an external agent. In Isa 28:27 the threshing wheel is 'turned' over cummin; Num 32:38 notes cities whose names 'were changed.' Arabic ghuyyira ('was changed') corresponds precisely. The passive implies an unnamed agent effecting the transformation — a grammatical reflex of the Hifil causative in sense 4.

gloss_terse: Draw near, approach; bring near or present — covering physical approach, cultic offering, and pressing forward
gloss_readable: A near-synonym of qarab but with its own distinctive profile, nagash emphasizes the deliberate, often momentous act of approaching. Abraham 'drew near' to plead for Sodom (Gen 18:23); Jacob 'drew near' for his father's blessing (Gen 27:22). In the Hifil, it takes on cultic force — to 'bring near' an offering before God (1 Sam 13:9). The Niphal carries a reflexive solemnity: presenting oneself for judgment or covenant (Exod 24:2). Across its 125 occurrences, nagash marks approach as a volitional, consequential act — one does not drift into God's presence but deliberately steps forward.

senses.1: The basic Qal sense: to draw near, approach, come close to a person or place. Spanish 'se acerco' and French 'approcha' consistently render this straightforward physical approach. Abraham approaches God in Gen 18:23; Jacob approaches Isaac in Gen 27:21-22. With 66 occurrences this is the dominant sense, covering approach in dialogue, deception, warfare, and worship alike.
senses.2: Hifil causative: to bring someone or something near, to bring forward. In Gen 27:25 Jacob 'brings near' food to Isaac; in Gen 48:10-13 Joseph 'brings his sons near' for blessing. Spanish 'acercame' and French 'apporte pres' highlight the transitive agency. This sense governs scenes of presentation — a person bringing another into the presence of someone greater.
senses.3: Niphal reflexive: to approach or present oneself, often with formal or solemn overtones. Exod 24:2 stipulates that Moses alone shall 'approach' the Lord; Exod 34:32 has the people 'approach' after Moses descends. The Niphal adds a self-presenting quality absent from the simple Qal — one readies and then advances. Spanish 'se acercaran' preserves this middle-voice dignity.
senses.4: Hifil specialized for cultic offering: to present or offer a sacrifice, gift, or tribute before God. Judges 6:19 has Gideon 'presenting' his offering; 1 Sam 13:9 has Saul 'bringing near' the burnt offering. French 'apportant' and Spanish 'presentando' isolate the ritual connotation. This sense bridges physical approach and sacred transaction — what is brought near becomes consecrated.
senses.5: Hofal passive: to be brought near or be offered. In Mal 1:11 incense 'is offered' to God's name among the nations; 2 Sam 3:34 notes Abner's hands 'were not brought near' (bound). Only two occurrences survive, both emphasizing the subject's passivity — it is acted upon by an unnamed agent performing the Hifil action of sense 2 or 4.
senses.6: A Qal sub-sense with aggressive or confrontational force: to advance, press forward. In Gen 19:9 the men of Sodom 'press forward' against Lot; Jer 46:3 commands warriors to 'advance' with shield and spear. Spanish 'acercaos' and English 'advance' capture the assertive momentum. The spatial approach of sense 1 acquires urgency and potential violence.
senses.7: A single occurrence in Isa 45:20 — an imperative calling the nations to 'draw near' for a divine disputation. Multilingual evidence (English 'draw near,' Spanish 'acercaos,' French 's'approcher') treats it as standard Qal approach, but the forensic and eschatological context — God summoning idol-worshippers to trial — gives it a distinctive juridical coloring not fully captured by sense 1.
senses.8: In Amos 9:13 the harvest 'overtakes' the reaper — an agricultural metaphor where approach becomes overtaking. Spanish 'alcanzara' ('will overtake') and French 's'approcher' show the semantic stretch: drawing near collapses into catching up with and surpassing. The eschatological abundance is so great that one season's work has not ended before the next arrives.
senses.9: In Amos 9:10 sinners claim disaster 'will not overtake' them. As in sense 8, nagash extends from approach to overtaking, but here with threatening force — calamity as a pursuer that 'draws near' and seizes. Spanish 'se acercara' retains the approach metaphor while English 'will overtake' completes the extension. Together with sense 8, these form a distinctive Amos-specific idiom.
